stem: A newborn boy has no kidney in either normal flank position on abdominal ultrasound. Instead, a single U-shaped band of normal-appearing renal tissue lies in the midline, just above the aortic bifurcation. Urine output is normal.
oneliner: Newborn M + no kidney in either normal flank + U-shaped renal tissue crossing the midline near the aortic bifurcation → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **one kidney sits low in the pelvis**; the other stays in its normal flank. Here the tissue is a single midline U-shaped mass
whyNot.B: **no renal tissue at all** and Potter sequence with oligohydramnios; here functioning tissue is present and urine output is normal
whyNot.D: **solid tumor mass** in a normally placed kidney, in an older child; this is a fused organ of normal texture
whyNot.E: **nonfunctioning kidney replaced by cysts** on one side; here there is one fused, solid U-shaped structure

why: **Fused U-shaped renal tissue in the midline near the aortic bifurcation** with no kidneys in the normal positions = horseshoe kidney (lower poles fuse; ascent is blocked by the inferior mesenteric artery).

stem: A 69-year-old man is undergoing elective repair of an abdominal aortic aneurysm. The surgeon finds that the lower poles of both kidneys are joined by a band of tissue that crosses the midline in front of the aorta. Each kidney is on its own side of the spine.
oneliner: 69M + AAA repair + both kidneys joined across the midline by a band in front of the aorta → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **both kidneys lie on the same side** and are fused; here each kidney is on its own side
whyNot.C: **kidney stuck low in the pelvis**, not joined to the other kidney across the midline
whyNot.D: **one kidney missing** with the other enlarged; here two kidneys are present
whyNot.E: **mass lesion** within one kidney; here the tissue is a band joining two normal kidneys

why: **Isthmus joining the lower poles across the midline, anterior to the aorta** = horseshoe kidney, the most common renal fusion anomaly.

stem: A 27-year-old man is evaluated as a possible kidney donor for his brother. Ultrasound shows no right kidney in the renal fossa and an enlarged left kidney. CT of the abdomen and pelvis shows no kidney anywhere else, and his creatinine is normal.
oneliner: 27M + no right kidney in the fossa + enlarged left kidney + nothing in the pelvis on CT → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **kidney present but low in the pelvis**; here CT finds no kidney anywhere
whyNot.B: **two fused kidneys** with a midline isthmus; here the left kidney is a single enlarged organ
whyNot.C: **small kidney is still present** on that side; here the right side holds no renal tissue
whyNot.D: **cystic, nonfunctioning kidney** visible on the affected side; here nothing is seen in the fossa

why: **Empty renal fossa, no ectopic kidney, compensatory hypertrophy of the other kidney** = unilateral renal agenesis (ureteric bud fails to induce the metanephric mesenchyme).

stem: A routine ultrasound at 32 weeks shows a male fetus with a markedly dilated left renal pelvis and calyces and a thin cortex. The left ureter is not seen, the bladder looks normal, the right kidney is normal, and the amniotic fluid volume is normal.
oneliner: Male fetus + one dilated renal pelvis, ureter not seen + normal bladder + normal amniotic fluid → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **bilateral** hydronephrosis, thick distended bladder and **oligohydramnios**; here only one side is affected with a normal bladder and fluid
whyNot.C: **dilated ureter** and intermittent changes; here the ureter is not dilated
whyNot.D: **no kidney at all**; here the left kidney is present and dilated
whyNot.E: **disorganized cysts** replace the kidney; here the pelvis and calyces are dilated in a connected pattern

why: **One dilated collecting system with no ureteral dilation, normal bladder and amniotic fluid** = blockage at the ureteropelvic junction, the most common cause of neonatal hydronephrosis.

stem: A 4-year-old boy has had two urinary tract infections and intermittent left flank pain after drinking large amounts of fluid. Ultrasound shows a dilated left renal pelvis and calyces with a normal ureter and bladder. A voiding cystourethrogram shows no reflux.
oneliner: 4M + recurrent UTI + left flank pain after big fluid intake + dilated pelvis, normal ureter + no reflux on VCUG → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **contrast refluxes up the ureter** on VCUG; here there is no reflux
whyNot.B: **dilated ureter above the stone**; here the ureter is normal and only the pelvis is dilated
whyNot.C: **bilateral** hydronephrosis with a thick-walled bladder and a dilated posterior urethra; here one side only and normal bladder
whyNot.E: **palpable solid mass** and hematuria or hypertension; here the collecting system is dilated, not replaced by tumor

why: **Flank pain after a fluid load, dilated pelvis with a normal ureter and bladder, and no reflux** = ureteropelvic junction obstruction.

stem: A 44-year-old woman has hypertension and recurrent flank pain with gross hematuria. Her mother and maternal uncle died of kidney failure, and her grandfather died of a ruptured berry aneurysm. CT shows both kidneys enlarged and filled with multiple cysts.
oneliner: 44F + hypertension + flank pain, hematuria + mother and uncle with renal failure + grandfather's berry aneurysm + enlarged cystic kidneys → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **presents in infancy** with Potter sequence and liver fibrosis; this adult has a dominant-pattern family history
whyNot.C: **angiomyolipomas**, seizures and skin lesions; no such features here
whyNot.D: **small kidneys** with cysts at the corticomedullary junction; here the kidneys are enlarged
whyNot.E: **single or few cysts**, no family history, normal function; here there are many cysts in both kidneys with familial disease

why: **Bilateral enlarged cystic kidneys, hypertension and family history of renal failure and berry aneurysm** = autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (PKD1/PKD2).

stem: A girl is born at 36 weeks after a pregnancy complicated by oligohydramnios. She has respiratory distress from birth, a flattened nose, a recessed chin, low-set ears and contractures of the limbs. Both flanks have a palpable mass. Ultrasound shows markedly enlarged, echogenic kidneys with tiny cysts. Her parents are healthy first cousins with normal kidney ultrasounds.
oneliner: Newborn F + oligohydramnios, respiratory distress, Potter facies + bilateral flank masses + large echogenic kidneys + healthy cousin parents with normal kidneys → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **usually presents in adulthood** with an affected parent who has cystic kidneys; here both parents have normal kidneys
whyNot.C: **no kidneys** and no palpable masses; here the kidneys are large
whyNot.D: **usually unilateral**, with a nonfunctioning kidney; here both kidneys are enlarged and uniformly echogenic
whyNot.E: **discrete solid mass** in a child, older than a newborn with Potter sequence; here both kidneys are diffusely enlarged

why: **Potter sequence with bilateral enlarged echogenic kidneys in a newborn of healthy consanguineous parents** = autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (PKHD1; associated with congenital hepatic fibrosis).

stem: A 27-year-old man has just finished a 5-hour trail run in warm weather and drank almost nothing during it. He is very thirsty, with dry mucous membranes, a heart rate of 112/min and a blood pressure of 100/62 mm Hg. Temperature is 37.4 C and mental status is normal. Serum sodium is 148 mEq/L and urine osmolality is 880 mOsm/kg.
oneliner: 27M + long run without fluids + thirst, dry mucosa, HR 112 + Na 148 + urine osm 880 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **dilute urine** with polyuria; here urine is highly concentrated
whyNot.B: **euvolemic hyponatremia** with concentrated urine; here sodium is high and he is volume depleted
whyNot.C: **excess water intake** with low sodium and dilute urine; here he drank little
whyNot.E: **core temperature above 40 C** and confusion; here temperature and mentation are normal

why: **Fluid loss without intake, high sodium and maximally concentrated urine (ADH acting on the collecting duct)** = dehydration.

stem: A 19-year-old wrestler tries to lose 4 kg in 2 days by using a sauna and laxatives and drinking nothing. He is light-headed on standing. Pulse is 118/min and blood pressure 88/52 mm Hg; temperature is normal and mucous membranes are dry. Labs: sodium 147 mEq/L, BUN 38 mg/dL, creatinine 1.3 mg/dL, hematocrit 52%, urine sodium 8 mEq/L, urine osmolality 820 mOsm/kg, creatine kinase 140 U/L. The urine sediment is bland.
oneliner: 19M + rapid weight cutting with sauna and laxatives + HR 118, BP 88/52 + BUN:Cr 29, urine Na 8, urine osm 820 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **core temperature above 40 C** with neurologic changes; here temperature is normal
whyNot.B: **CK in the thousands** and pigmented urine; here CK is normal and sediment is bland
whyNot.C: **muddy brown casts and urine sodium above 40**; here sodium is 8 and the sediment is bland
whyNot.D: **low serum sodium** in a euvolemic patient; here sodium is high and he is hypovolemic

why: **Orthostatic tachycardia, BUN:Cr near 30, low urine sodium and concentrated urine after fluid loss** = volume depletion (prerenal state).

stem: A 30-year-old man with a stab wound to the thigh has lost about 1 L of blood. Blood pressure is 88/58 mm Hg with a heart rate of 124/min, flat neck veins, cool skin and no rash or wheeze; plasma renin activity is high.
oneliner: 30M + stab wound with ~1 L blood loss + BP 88/58, HR 124, flat neck veins + high renin → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **distended neck veins** and pulmonary congestion; here neck veins are flat
whyNot.B: **fever** and warm skin from vasodilation; here the skin is cool and there is a clear bleeding source
whyNot.D: **bradycardia with warm, dry skin** after spinal injury; here he is tachycardic and cool
whyNot.E: **urticaria, wheeze or angioedema** after an allergen exposure; none here

why: **Blood loss, flat neck veins, cool skin and tachycardia with high renin** = hypovolemic shock.

stem: A 34-year-old woman finishes her first marathon in 5 hours after drinking water at every aid station. Thirty minutes later she has a headache, nausea and new confusion. Her weight is 2 kg above her pre-race weight. Temperature is 37.0 C, pulse 96/min and blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg. Serum potassium is 4.0 mEq/L and glucose 92 mg/dL.
oneliner: 34F + marathon with water at every station + 2 kg weight gain + headache, confusion + normal temp, K and glucose → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **core temperature above 40 C** with hot, dry skin; here temperature is normal
whyNot.B: **weight loss and thirst**; she gained 2 kg after drinking heavily
whyNot.C: **hyperkalemia** and hypotension; here potassium is normal and blood pressure is fine
whyNot.D: **chronic compulsive water drinking** in a psychiatric patient; here the water load is tied to the race and there is no such history

why: **Confusion after heavy water drinking with weight gain during a long race** = exercise-associated (dilutional) hyponatremia.

stem: A 63-year-old woman with hypertension takes hydrochlorothiazide. Over 3 weeks she has developed muscle cramps, generalized weakness and constipation. Examination is otherwise normal. An ECG shows flattened T waves and prominent U waves. Labs: sodium 138 mEq/L, calcium 9.4 mg/dL, bicarbonate 29 mEq/L, TSH normal, plasma renin activity and aldosterone normal.
oneliner: 63F + hydrochlorothiazide + cramps, weakness, constipation + ECG flat T waves, U waves + normal Na, Ca, TSH, aldosterone → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **high serum calcium** causes constipation and weakness; here calcium is 9.4
whyNot.C: **raised TSH** with cold intolerance and slowing; TSH is normal here
whyNot.D: **high aldosterone with suppressed renin**; both are normal here, and the thiazide explains the potassium loss
whyNot.E: **low serum sodium** with confusion or seizures; sodium is 138 here

why: **Thiazide use with cramps, weakness, constipation and U waves on ECG**, with normal calcium, TSH and aldosterone = hypokalemia.

stem: A 41-year-old man has had profuse watery diarrhea for 7 days. He is tachycardic with dry mucous membranes. Labs: sodium 138 mEq/L, potassium 3.1 mEq/L, chloride 114 mEq/L, bicarbonate 14 mEq/L, glucose 94 mg/dL, lactate 1.0 mmol/L, serum ketones negative. Arterial pH is 7.28 and PCO2 is 30 mm Hg. Urine anion gap is negative.
oneliner: 41M + diarrhea 7 d + Na 138, Cl 114, HCO3 14 (gap 10) + pH 7.28, PCO2 30 + negative urine anion gap → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **raised anion gap** with high lactate; the gap is 10 and lactate is 1.0
whyNot.B: **raised anion gap**, high glucose and ketones; glucose is 94 and ketones are negative
whyNot.D: **high pH** with a low PCO2 as the primary problem; here pH is low and the low PCO2 is compensation
whyNot.E: **positive urine anion gap** because the kidney cannot excrete ammonium; here the gap is negative

answer: Non-anion gap metabolic acidosis from diarrheal bicarbonate loss
why: **Normal anion gap (10), low bicarbonate, high chloride and a negative urine anion gap after diarrhea** = non-anion gap metabolic acidosis from GI bicarbonate loss.

stem: A 62-year-old man with chronic kidney disease and heart failure has leg edema and fatigue. Labs: sodium 138 mEq/L, chloride 103 mEq/L, bicarbonate 17 mEq/L, BUN 100 mg/dL, creatinine 8.4 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas on room air: pH 7.29, PCO2 32 mm Hg, PO2 94 mm Hg.
oneliner: 62M + CKD and heart failure with edema + BUN 100, Cr 8.4 + HCO3 17 + pH 7.29, PCO2 32 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **high pH** from hyperventilation; here pH is 7.29, so the low PCO2 is compensation
whyNot.C: **high PCO2** with low pH; here PCO2 is low
whyNot.D: **high pH and high bicarbonate**; here bicarbonate is 17 and pH is low
whyNot.E: **PCO2 above the expected value** (about 33 by Winter's formula); here PCO2 of 32 is appropriately low

why: **Low pH, low bicarbonate and a low PCO2 that matches the expected compensation** in advanced renal failure = metabolic acidosis.

stem: A 25-year-old woman has fatigue and fast breathing. She has no vomiting, diarrhea, laxative use or medications. Labs: sodium 139 mEq/L, potassium 3.2 mEq/L, chloride 112 mEq/L, bicarbonate 15 mEq/L, glucose 88 mg/dL, lactate normal, salicylate level undetectable. Arterial pH is 7.25. Urine pH is 6.6 and the urine anion gap is positive.
oneliner: 25F + fast breathing + Cl 112, HCO3 15, normal gap, pH 7.25 + urine pH 6.6, positive urine anion gap, no GI losses → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **raised anion gap with high glucose and ketones**; glucose is 88 and the gap is normal
whyNot.B: **raised anion gap** and high lactate; the gap is normal and lactate is normal
whyNot.C: **detectable salicylate** with a raised gap and respiratory alkalosis; level is undetectable
whyNot.E: **negative urine anion gap** and a history of GI loss; here the gap is positive and she has no diarrhea

why: **Hyperchloremic normal-gap acidosis with an inappropriately high urine pH and a positive urine anion gap** = renal tubular acidosis (kidney cannot excrete acid).

stem: An 8-year-old girl has poor growth and has needed alkali therapy since toddlerhood for hyperchloremic acidosis. Serum potassium is 2.9 mEq/L with a normal anion gap. Urine pH is 6.8 even when she is acidotic, and kidney ultrasound shows nephrocalcinosis. Urine glucose and amino acids are normal.
oneliner: 8F + poor growth + hyperchloremic acidosis on alkali since toddler + K 2.9 + urine pH 6.8 despite acidosis + nephrocalcinosis → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **urine pH falls below 5.3 once bicarbonate is low** and nephrocalcinosis is absent; here urine stays alkaline with calcium deposits
whyNot.C: **high potassium** from low aldosterone effect; here potassium is low
whyNot.D: **glucosuria and aminoaciduria**; here urine glucose and amino acids are normal
whyNot.E: **metabolic alkalosis** with hypokalemia; here she has acidosis

why: **Persistently alkaline urine despite acidosis, low potassium and nephrocalcinosis** = distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis (failure of alpha-intercalated cells to secrete H+).

stem: A 12-year-old girl has bone pain and polyuria. Labs: sodium 137 mEq/L, potassium 3.0 mEq/L, chloride 111 mEq/L, bicarbonate 15 mEq/L, phosphate 1.8 mg/dL, uric acid 1.9 mg/dL, glucose 85 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows glucose, and urine amino acids and phosphate are high. Urine pH is 5.0.
oneliner: 12F + bone pain, polyuria + normal-gap acidosis, low phosphate and uric acid + glucosuria with glucose 85 + aminoaciduria → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **urine pH above 5.5** and no glucose, amino acid or phosphate wasting; here urine pH is 5.0 with multiple solute losses
whyNot.C: **hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis**; here bicarbonate is low
whyNot.D: **hypomagnesemia and hypocalciuria** with alkalosis; here there is acidosis and phosphate wasting
whyNot.E: **serum glucose is high** when glucose is in the urine; here glucose is 85

why: **Combined loss of bicarbonate, phosphate, amino acids, glucose and uric acid with a normal serum glucose** = Fanconi syndrome (global proximal tubule dysfunction).

stem: A 38-year-old woman with bipolar disorder, treated with lithium for 8 years, reports drinking and urinating large volumes; urine output is 6 L/day. Labs: serum sodium 146 mEq/L, plasma osmolality 302 mOsm/kg, glucose 90 mg/dL. Urine osmolality is 110 mOsm/kg at baseline, 140 after overnight water restriction, and 150 after desmopressin.
oneliner: 38F + lithium for 8 y + polyuria 6 L/d + Na 146 + urine osm 140 after water restriction, 150 after desmopressin → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **urine osmolality rises more than 50% after desmopressin**; here it barely changes
whyNot.B: **urine concentrates after water restriction** and sodium is low-normal; here urine stays dilute and sodium is high
whyNot.C: **concentrated urine with low sodium**; here urine is dilute and sodium is high
whyNot.E: **glucosuria and high serum glucose** cause osmotic diuresis; glucose is 90

why: **Dilute urine that does not respond to water restriction or desmopressin on lithium** = nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

stem: A 10-month-old boy has poor weight gain, irritability, vomiting and constant wet diapers. His mother's brother had similar symptoms in infancy. Labs: serum sodium 156 mEq/L, plasma osmolality 322 mOsm/kg, calcium 9.8 mg/dL. Urine osmolality is 90 mOsm/kg and stays at 90 after supervised water restriction and 95 after vasopressin.
oneliner: 10-month M + poor feeding, polyuria, irritability + affected maternal uncle + Na 156, normal Ca + urine osm stays 90-95 after water restriction and vasopressin → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **urine becomes concentrated after vasopressin**; here there is no response
whyNot.B: **urine concentrates with water restriction**, sodium low-normal; here sodium is 156 and urine stays dilute
whyNot.D: **concentrated urine and low sodium**; here urine is dilute and sodium is high
whyNot.E: **high serum calcium** can cause polyuria, but his calcium is 9.8; the X-linked family pattern and no response to vasopressin fit a receptor defect

answer: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (X-linked, V2 receptor defect)
why: **Maternal-uncle pattern and no urine concentration after vasopressin** = congenital nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (V2 receptor loss of function).

stem: A 45-year-old man has puffy eyes and pitting leg edema. Blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg, neck veins are flat, the lungs are clear, and there is no ascites. Labs: serum albumin 1.9 g/dL, LDL cholesterol 240 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows protein excretion of 6.5 g/24 h, fat droplets and no red cell casts.
oneliner: 45M + periorbital and leg edema + normal BP, flat neck veins + albumin 1.9 + proteinuria 6.5 g/d + no RBC casts → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **hypertension, hematuria and RBC casts** with limited proteinuria; here BP is normal and there are no red cell casts
whyNot.C: **raised neck veins, crackles** and normal albumin; here neck veins are flat and albumin is very low
whyNot.D: **ascites, hepatomegaly** and a normal urinalysis; here there is no ascites and heavy proteinuria
whyNot.E: **non-pitting, often asymmetric** edema with normal albumin; here edema pits and albumin is 1.9

why: **Proteinuria above 3.5 g/day, hypoalbuminemia, hyperlipidemia and edema with normal pressure and no casts** = nephrotic syndrome (low plasma oncotic pressure drives the edema).

stem: A 5-year-old boy has had puffy eyelids for a week, followed by swelling of the legs and abdomen. Blood pressure is normal. Urinalysis shows 4+ protein and no blood; creatinine and C3 are normal. A PAS-stained kidney biopsy is shown.
oneliner: 5M + periorbital then generalized edema + 4+ protein, no hematuria + normal creatinine and C3 + [PAS-stained biopsy]
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **segmental scars in some glomeruli** on light microscopy; the glomerulus shown has none
whyNot.B: **diffusely thickened capillary walls**, mostly in adults; the walls here are thin
whyNot.C: **hematuria, low C3** and hypercellular glomeruli; he has no blood and C3 is normal
whyNot.D: **tram-track basement membranes** and low C3; the picture shows neither

why: **Child with nephrotic-range proteinuria, no hematuria, normal C3 and a normal-looking glomerulus on light microscopy** = minimal change disease (podocyte foot-process effacement only on electron microscopy).

image.prompt: A high-power PAS-stained kidney biopsy showing a single glomerulus with normal cellularity, thin delicate capillary loops, open capillary lumens and a normal mesangium, surrounded by normal tubules. No sclerosis, no deposits and no crescents.

stem: A 48-year-old man has leg edema and a urine protein excretion of 7 g/day with no hematuria; he has no rash or joint pain. Kidney biopsy shows diffusely thickened glomerular capillary walls without increased cellularity. Immunofluorescence shows granular IgG and C3 along the capillary loops, and electron microscopy shows subepithelial deposits.
oneliner: 48M + nephrotic syndrome + diffuse thick capillary walls + granular IgG/C3 + subepithelial deposits → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **normal glomeruli** and no immune deposits on immunofluorescence; here walls are thick with deposits
whyNot.B: **segmental scarring** and negative or non-specific immunofluorescence; here the thickening is diffuse with granular IgG
whyNot.C: **'full-house' staining (IgG, IgA, IgM, C1q)** with systemic features; here only IgG and C3 and no rash or arthritis
whyNot.E: **apple-green Congo red birefringence** and non-immune fibrils; not described and the deposits are immune complexes

why: **Diffuse thick basement membrane with granular IgG/C3 and subepithelial deposits in an adult with nephrotic syndrome** = membranous nephropathy (spike and dome pattern).

stem: A 58-year-old man has had type 1 diabetes for 22 years. He now has urine protein excretion of 3.5 g/day and a rising creatinine. A PAS-stained kidney biopsy is shown.
oneliner: 58M + type 1 diabetes for 22 y + proteinuria 3.5 g/d + [PAS-stained biopsy]
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **hyaline arteriolosclerosis** and shrunken glomeruli with mild proteinuria; the glomerulus here shows large rounded nodules
whyNot.C: **Congo red apple-green deposits** of amorphous fibrils; the nodules here are PAS-positive mesangial matrix
whyNot.D: **diffuse thick capillary walls** with no nodules; here the mesangium is nodular
whyNot.E: **segmental scars** with no nodules; here the sclerosis is global and nodular

why: **Long-standing diabetes with proteinuria and nodular mesangial sclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules)** = diabetic nephropathy.

image.prompt: A PAS-stained glomerulus with several large, rounded, pale-pink acellular nodules in the mesangium, thickened capillary basement membranes, and a thickened hyaline afferent arteriole nearby. No crescents and no hypercellularity.

stem: A 55-year-old woman has had type 2 diabetes for 12 years, with background retinopathy on eye examination. Blood pressure is 148/90 mm Hg. Her urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio is 450 mg/g with no red cells, and kidney ultrasound shows normal-sized kidneys.
oneliner: 55F + type 2 diabetes 12 y + retinopathy + albuminuria 450 mg/g, no hematuria + normal-sized kidneys → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **small, scarred kidneys** and mild proteinuria after long uncontrolled hypertension; here BP is only mildly raised, kidneys are normal-sized and retinopathy points to diabetes
whyNot.B: **nephrotic syndrome** in an adult, often with a secondary cause; here diabetes and retinopathy better explain albuminuria
whyNot.D: **heavy proteinuria with segmental scars**, often obesity or HIV; no such cues here
whyNot.E: **large kidneys, macroglossia, neuropathy** and a plasma cell or inflammatory disorder; none here

why: **Long-standing diabetes with retinopathy, albuminuria, no hematuria and normal-sized kidneys** = diabetic nephropathy.

stem: A 7-year-old boy has dark, cola-colored urine and puffy eyelids 2 weeks after a sore throat. Blood pressure is 142/92 mm Hg. Urinalysis shows red cell casts and mild proteinuria, and serum C3 is low.
oneliner: 7M + cola urine + periorbital edema 2 weeks after sore throat + BP 142/92 + RBC casts + low C3 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **hematuria 1-2 days after the infection** with normal C3; here the delay is 2 weeks and C3 is low
whyNot.B: **heavy proteinuria without blood**; here there are RBC casts and hypertension
whyNot.C: **family history, hearing loss** and normal C3; none here
whyNot.D: **WBC casts after a new drug**, often with rash; here there are RBC casts after a sore throat

why: **Nephritic urine with RBC casts, hypertension and low C3 two weeks after pharyngitis** = poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (immune-complex, subepithelial humps).

stem: A 22-year-old man has episodes of tea-colored urine that begin 1 to 2 days into every cold. He has no rash or joint pain, urine shows RBC casts, and serum C3 is normal.
oneliner: 22M + tea-colored urine 1-2 d into each URI + RBC casts + normal C3, no rash → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **weeks after infection** with low C3; here hematuria starts within 1-2 days and C3 is normal
whyNot.C: **hearing loss and family history** of renal failure; none described
whyNot.D: **palpable purpura, abdominal pain, arthralgia**; he has no rash or joint pain
whyNot.E: **benign familial hematuria** without RBC casts or episodic flares with infection

why: **Hematuria within 1-2 days of an upper respiratory infection, RBC casts and normal C3** = IgA nephropathy (mesangial IgA deposits).

stem: A 26-year-old woman is found to have blood in her urine at a routine job screening. She feels well and blood pressure is normal. Urinalysis shows red cells with rare red cell casts and no protein. ASO titer, C3 and creatinine are normal, and no family member has kidney disease or deafness.
oneliner: 26F + incidental hematuria + rare RBC casts + no proteinuria + negative ASO, normal C3 + no family history → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **recent infection, low C3 and raised ASO**; here ASO and C3 are normal
whyNot.B: **heavy proteinuria**; urine here has no protein
whyNot.C: **systemic features, low C3 and proteinuria**; she is well, C3 is normal and there is no protein
whyNot.E: **family history, deafness or eye findings**; she has none

why: **Isolated glomerular hematuria with RBC casts, no proteinuria, normal C3 and negative ASO** = IgA nephropathy, the most common glomerular cause of isolated hematuria.

stem: A 24-year-old man who smokes has had 3 days of coughing up blood and 2 weeks of dark urine. Creatinine is 3.6 mg/dL, and urinalysis shows red cell casts. ANCA testing is negative. Kidney biopsy immunofluorescence shows linear IgG staining along the glomerular capillary loops.
oneliner: 24M smoker + hemoptysis + dark urine + creatinine 3.6, RBC casts + ANCA negative + linear IgG on biopsy → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **ANCA positive**, sinus disease and a pauci-immune biopsy; here ANCA is negative and IgG is linear
whyNot.C: **mesangial granular IgA** without lung bleeding; here the staining is linear IgG with hemoptysis
whyNot.D: **granular 'full-house'** immunofluorescence and systemic features; here the staining is linear
whyNot.E: **lumpy-bumpy subepithelial humps** after strep infection with no lung bleeding; here staining is linear

why: **Hemoptysis plus rapidly progressive nephritis with linear IgG along the basement membrane** = Goodpasture syndrome (antibodies to type IV collagen alpha-3 chain).

stem: A 12-year-old boy has recurrent hematuria and bilateral high-frequency hearing loss. His maternal uncle needed dialysis in his 30s; the boy has no burning pain in his hands or feet and no skin lesions.
oneliner: 12M + hematuria + sensorineural hearing loss + maternal uncle on dialysis + no limb pain or skin lesions → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **benign hematuria** with normal hearing and normal long-term renal function; here there is deafness and renal failure in a relative
whyNot.B: **episodes with infections** and no deafness or X-linked family pattern
whyNot.D: **acroparesthesias and angiokeratomas**; he has no pain or skin lesions
whyNot.E: **one-time illness weeks after strep** with low C3; this boy has recurrent hematuria and a family pattern

why: **Hematuria, sensorineural deafness and X-linked family history of renal failure** = Alport syndrome (type IV collagen defect).

stem: A 3-year-old girl has 4 days of bloody diarrhea after a picnic where undercooked ground beef was served. She is now pale and passing very little urine. Hemoglobin is 7.8 g/dL, platelets 40,000/mm3, and creatinine 2.4 mg/dL; the smear shows schistocytes. PT and PTT are normal, and she is alert and afebrile.
oneliner: 3F + bloody diarrhea after undercooked beef + pallor, oliguria + Hb 7.8, platelets 40,000, Cr 2.4, schistocytes + normal PT/PTT → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **fever and neurologic changes** in an adult, with severe ADAMTS13 deficiency; here the child is alert, afebrile and has bloody diarrhea with renal failure
whyNot.C: **prolonged PT and PTT** with low fibrinogen; both are normal here
whyNot.D: **isolated low platelets** without anemia, schistocytes or renal failure
whyNot.E: **bite cells and Heinz bodies** after an oxidant trigger, with normal platelets and kidneys

why: **Bloody diarrhea followed by microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, low platelets and acute kidney injury** = hemolytic uremic syndrome (Shiga toxin).

stem: A 72-year-old man with heart failure had his furosemide dose doubled a week ago and has been eating and drinking poorly. He is orthostatic with dry mucous membranes. Labs: BUN 62 mg/dL, creatinine 1.9 mg/dL (baseline 1.0), fractional excretion of sodium 0.4%, urine osmolality 520 mOsm/kg. Urinalysis shows only hyaline casts, and renal ultrasound is normal.
oneliner: 72M + doubled furosemide, poor intake + orthostasis + BUN 62, Cr 1.9 (BUN:Cr >30) + FENa 0.4% + only hyaline casts → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **FENa above 2%, muddy brown casts** and urine isosthenuria; here FENa is 0.4% and the sediment is bland
whyNot.B: **fever, rash, WBC casts and eosinophils**; none here and sediment is bland
whyNot.C: **hydronephrosis** on ultrasound; the ultrasound is normal
whyNot.D: **RBC casts and proteinuria**; the urine shows only hyaline casts

why: **Volume loss from a diuretic, BUN:Cr above 20, FENa below 1% and a bland sediment** = prerenal azotemia (kidney reabsorbs sodium and urea).

stem: A 70-year-old man with known bilateral renal artery stenosis starts taking ibuprofen 800 mg three times daily for knee pain. Three days later his creatinine has risen from 1.2 to 2.8 mg/dL and his urine output has dropped. He has no fever or rash, urine sediment is bland with no eosinophils, fractional excretion of sodium is 0.6%, and ultrasound shows no hydronephrosis.
oneliner: 70M + bilateral renal artery stenosis + new ibuprofen 800 mg TID + Cr 1.2 to 2.8 in 3 d + bland urine, FENa 0.6%, no hydronephrosis → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **fever, rash, eosinophiluria and WBC casts**; none here and sediment is bland
whyNot.C: **FENa above 2%** with muddy brown casts; here FENa is 0.6% and there are no casts
whyNot.D: **hydronephrosis**; ultrasound shows none
whyNot.E: **hematuria with RBC casts**; urine is bland

why: **NSAID-blocked prostaglandin afferent dilation in a kidney dependent on it, with low FENa and a bland sediment** = prerenal azotemia.

stem: A 34-year-old man in the intensive care unit has had septic shock with a blood pressure of 70/40 mm Hg for 18 hours. After fluids and vasopressors his pressure is restored, but urine output is 150 mL/day. Creatinine has risen from 1.0 to 3.8 mg/dL. Urine sodium is high with a fractional excretion of sodium of 4%, urine osmolality is 300 mOsm/kg, and the sediment shows muddy brown granular casts. He has no rash and no urine eosinophils.
oneliner: 34M + septic shock with BP 70/40 for 18 h + oliguria, Cr 1.0 to 3.8 + FENa 4%, urine osm 300 + muddy brown casts → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **FENa below 1%, concentrated urine, bland sediment** that corrects with volume; here FENa is 4% with casts
whyNot.B: **fever, rash, eosinophiluria** after a drug; he has no rash or urine eosinophils and the sediment shows muddy brown casts
whyNot.C: **low platelets, prolonged PT and bleeding**; renal injury here is explained by prolonged shock and casts
whyNot.E: **sudden anuria or flank pain** with no casts; here urine output falls after shock with granular casts

why: **Prolonged hypotension, oliguria, high FENa, isosthenuric urine and muddy brown casts** = acute tubular necrosis (ischemic injury; the metabolically active proximal tubule and thick ascending limb die first).

stem: A 66-year-old man is resuscitated after a cardiac arrest. Over the next 3 days urine output falls below 300 mL/day and creatinine peaks at 5.1 mg/dL despite intravenous fluids; urine contains granular casts and fractional excretion of sodium is 3%. In the second week urine output rises to 3 L/day while BUN is still high and creatinine gradually falls.
oneliner: 66M + cardiac arrest + oliguria, Cr peak 5.1 unresponsive to fluids + granular casts, FENa 3% + polyuria with recovery in week 2 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **FENa below 1% and rapid correction with fluids**; here fluids failed and FENa is 3%
whyNot.B: **fever, rash and eosinophiluria** after a drug; none here
whyNot.D: **RBC casts and proteinuria**; here granular casts and a recovery phase
whyNot.E: **flank pain, hematuria** and an enlarged kidney; none here

why: **Renal ischemia after cardiac arrest, granular casts, high FENa and a recovery polyuric phase** = acute tubular necrosis.

stem: A 29-year-old man was trapped under rubble for hours. Two days later urine output is 100 mL/day with dark brown urine that is dipstick-positive for blood but has no red cells, potassium is 6.3 mEq/L, and BUN is rising; he has no rash and his bladder is not palpable.
oneliner: 29M + crush injury 2 d ago + oliguria + brown urine, blood on dipstick but no RBCs + K 6.3, no rash, bladder not palpable → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **concentrated urine with FENa below 1%** that corrects with fluids; pigment casts from muscle breakdown point to tubular injury here
whyNot.B: **fever, rash and a new drug**; he has none
whyNot.C: **distended bladder or hydronephrosis**; the bladder is not palpable
whyNot.D: **red cells and RBC casts** in the urine; here there are no red cells

answer: Acute tubular necrosis (pigment nephropathy from rhabdomyolysis)
why: **Crush injury, myoglobin-type urine (heme-positive, no RBCs), oliguria and hyperkalemia** = acute tubular necrosis from rhabdomyolysis.

stem: A 72-year-old man is treated with gentamicin for 8 days for a catheter-associated urinary tract infection. His creatinine rises from 1.0 to 2.9 mg/dL while urine output stays near normal. The sediment shows muddy brown granular casts. He has no fever, rash, flank pain or eosinophiluria, and ultrasound shows no hydronephrosis.
oneliner: 72M + gentamicin 8 d for catheter UTI + Cr 1.0 to 2.9, urine output kept + muddy brown casts + no fever, rash or hydronephrosis → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **fever, flank pain and WBC casts**; none here
whyNot.C: **fever, rash and eosinophiluria**; he has none and shows muddy brown casts
whyNot.D: **bland sediment and FENa below 1%**; granular casts here point to tubular injury
whyNot.E: **hydronephrosis** on ultrasound; none present

why: **Aminoglycoside exposure followed by rising creatinine and muddy brown casts** = acute tubular necrosis (direct proximal tubule toxicity).

stem: A 45-year-old woman is treated with amoxicillin for sinusitis. Ten days later she has fever and a diffuse maculopapular rash, and creatinine has risen from 0.9 to 2.4 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows white cells, white cell casts and eosinophils, and the urine culture is sterile.
oneliner: 45F + amoxicillin 10 d ago + fever, rash + Cr 0.9 to 2.4 + WBC casts, urine eosinophils + sterile culture → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **muddy brown casts after ischemia or toxin** without fever or rash; here fever, rash and eosinophils follow a drug
whyNot.B: **positive urine culture** and flank pain; the culture here is sterile
whyNot.C: **RBC casts, hypertension and low C3**; here WBC casts and eosinophils
whyNot.E: **heavy proteinuria without fever, rash or WBC casts**

why: **Fever, rash and eosinophiluria with WBC casts after a beta-lactam** = acute interstitial nephritis (type IV hypersensitivity).

stem: A 63-year-old man has taken naproxen daily for 3 months for arthritis. He now has fatigue, creatinine of 2.1 mg/dL (baseline 0.9) and urine protein of 4 g/day with white cells and urine eosinophils. Kidney biopsy shows an interstitial infiltrate of lymphocytes and eosinophils with normal glomeruli on light microscopy and no papillary damage.
oneliner: 63M + naproxen daily 3 months + Cr 2.1 + proteinuria 4 g/d with WBCs, urine eosinophils + interstitial lymphocytes and eosinophils, normal glomeruli → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **decades of mixed analgesic use** with papillary necrosis; here 3 months of one drug and no papillary damage
whyNot.C: **thick capillary walls with subepithelial deposits**; the glomeruli here are normal
whyNot.D: **tubular cell injury with muddy brown casts**; here the infiltrate is interstitial
whyNot.E: **fever, flank pain and a neutrophil-rich infiltrate** with bacteria; here the infiltrate is lymphocytes and eosinophils

why: **Interstitial lymphocytes and eosinophils after NSAID exposure with pyuria and eosinophiluria** = acute interstitial nephritis (drug hypersensitivity).

stem: A 63-year-old woman has taken analgesic powders containing aspirin, acetaminophen and caffeine daily for 25 years for headaches. She has polyuria, mild proteinuria, sterile pyuria and a creatinine of 2.5 mg/dL. A photograph of the cut surface of one of her kidneys is shown.
oneliner: 63F + daily aspirin/acetaminophen powders for 25 y + polyuria, sterile pyuria + Cr 2.5 + [photo of kidney]
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **coarse scars over dilated blunted calyces** after repeated infections; here the damage is in the papillae with a history of analgesic use
whyNot.B: **fine granular surface** with hypertension and normal papillae
whyNot.D: **diabetes and nodular glomerulosclerosis**; she has no diabetes and the injury is papillary
whyNot.E: **large kidneys full of cysts**; the specimen is shrunken without cysts

why: **Years of combined analgesic use with scarred kidneys and necrotic, sloughed papillae and poor concentrating ability** = analgesic nephropathy (chronic papillary necrosis).

image.prompt: A cut section of a small, shrunken kidney with an irregular, scarred surface and thinned cortex. The renal papillae are ragged, brown-gray and necrotic, with some sloughed away, leaving blunted pale calyces.

stem: A 19-year-old man with sickle cell disease has flank pain and gross hematuria. He passes a small fragment of gray-brown tissue in his urine. Temperature is normal, urine culture is negative, and CT shows no stones, no mass and no hydronephrosis. Creatinine is 1.3 mg/dL.
oneliner: 19M + sickle cell disease + flank pain + gross hematuria + passed tissue fragment + negative culture, CT without stone or mass → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **fever, pyuria with bacteria and a positive culture**; he is afebrile with a negative culture
whyNot.C: **stone on CT** with colic; CT here shows no stone
whyNot.D: **oliguria and muddy brown casts**; here hematuria with a passed tissue fragment
whyNot.E: **painless hematuria in older smokers** with a mass or filling defect; he is young with no mass

why: **Sickle cell disease with flank pain, hematuria and a passed sloughed papilla** = renal papillary necrosis (hypoxic medulla).

stem: A 58-year-old man with 20 years of diabetes and hypertension has fatigue, bone pain and itching. His eGFR is 14 mL/min/1.73 m2. Labs: calcium 7.5 mg/dL, phosphate 7.2 mg/dL, intact PTH 520 pg/mL (normal 10-65), alkaline phosphatase elevated, 25-hydroxyvitamin D normal at 32 ng/mL.
oneliner: 58M + diabetes and hypertension 20 y + bone pain, itching + eGFR 14 + Ca 7.5, phosphate 7.2, PTH 520, normal 25-OH vitamin D → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.E: Secondary hyperparathyroidism of chronic kidney disease

whyNot.A: **high calcium and low phosphate** with high PTH; here calcium is low and phosphate high
whyNot.B: **low 25-hydroxyvitamin D** with low phosphate; here the level is normal and phosphate is high
whyNot.C: **low PTH** with low calcium; here PTH is very high
whyNot.D: **PTH resistance with normal kidney function**; here eGFR is 14

answer: Secondary hyperparathyroidism of chronic kidney disease (renal osteodystrophy)
why: **Low eGFR with low calcium, high phosphate, high PTH and normal 25-OH vitamin D** = chronic kidney disease (failure to make calcitriol and clear phosphate drives secondary hyperparathyroidism).

stem: A 55-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease on hemodialysis has missed his last three sessions. Over 4 days he has developed nausea, intense itching and confusion. He has excoriations on the arms and has gained 4 kg. BUN is 148 mg/dL, creatinine 11.2 mg/dL, potassium 4.8 mEq/L, and TSH is normal.
oneliner: 55M + ESRD, missed dialysis x3 + nausea, itching with excoriations, confusion, 4 kg gain + BUN 148, Cr 11.2, K 4.8 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **low mood and anhedonia** without itching or nitrogen retention; BUN 148 here explains the picture
whyNot.C: **raised TSH**, cold intolerance, bradycardia; TSH is normal here
whyNot.D: **weakness and ECG changes** with raised potassium; potassium here is 4.8
whyNot.E: **cirrhosis stigmata** and high ammonia; he has end-stage kidney disease and no liver disease

why: **Missed dialysis, markedly raised BUN and creatinine with pruritus, nausea, confusion and volume gain** = uremia from end-stage chronic kidney disease.

stem: A 52-year-old man with diabetic kidney disease is on hemodialysis. His blood pressure has been controlled at 130/80 mm Hg on two drugs. Three weeks after starting epoetin for anemia, hemoglobin rose from 8.2 to 10.4 g/dL and blood pressure is now 168/102 mm Hg. His dry weight is unchanged, he has no edema, no episodic sweating or palpitations, and no abdominal bruit.
oneliner: 52M + hemodialysis + BP 130/80 controlled + 3 weeks after starting epoetin, BP 168/102 + stable dry weight, no edema, bruit or episodic symptoms → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient's rise in blood pressure?

options.D: Erythropoietin-induced hypertension in chronic kidney disease

whyNot.A: **weight gain above dry weight and edema**; his weight is stable and he has no edema
whyNot.B: **abdominal bruit** and a gradual rise; he has no bruit and the rise follows a new drug
whyNot.C: **episodic sweating, palpitations and headache**; none here
whyNot.E: **gradual** bone and mineral changes, not a sudden rise in pressure that follows a new drug

why: **BP rise that begins weeks after starting epoetin with stable weight and no other cause** = erythropoietin-induced hypertension in chronic kidney disease (raised hematocrit and vasoconstriction).

stem: A 38-year-old woman received a deceased-donor kidney transplant 4 months ago. She now has a temperature of 38.2 C, a tender swollen graft, and creatinine that has risen from 1.1 to 2.2 mg/dL over 3 days. Her tacrolimus level is in the target range. Biopsy shows lymphocytes invading the tubular epithelium.
oneliner: 38F + deceased-donor kidney 4 months ago + fever, tender graft + Cr 1.1 to 2.2 in 3 d + normal tacrolimus level + lymphocytic tubulitis on biopsy → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **minutes to hours after anastomosis** from preformed antibodies; this is 4 months out
whyNot.B: **slow decline over years** with vascular fibrosis; here creatinine doubled in 3 days with fever and graft tenderness
whyNot.D: **high drug level** and vacuolized tubules with no tenderness or tubulitis; here the level is therapeutic
whyNot.E: **proteinuria or hematuria** with glomerular changes; the biopsy shows lymphocytes in the tubules

why: **Months after transplant with fever, graft tenderness, rapid creatinine rise and lymphocytic tubulitis** = acute cellular rejection (T-cell mediated).

stem: A 66-year-old man with coronary disease and intermittent claudication has a new blood pressure of 200/115 mm Hg; it was normal a year ago. A systolic bruit is heard over the upper abdomen. Labs: creatinine 1.5 mg/dL, potassium 4.1 mEq/L, plasma renin activity 9 ng/mL/h (elevated), TSH normal. There is no pulsatile mass and no episodic headache or sweating.
oneliner: 66M + coronary disease and claudication + new BP 200/115 + systolic abdominal bruit + high renin, normal K and TSH → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **episodic headache, sweating and palpitations** with raised metanephrines; none here and renin is high
whyNot.C: **pulsatile abdominal mass**; he has none
whyNot.D: **low renin with hypokalemia**; renin here is high and potassium is normal
whyNot.E: **tremor, weight loss and isolated systolic hypertension** with low TSH; TSH is normal

why: **Sudden hypertension in an atherosclerotic older man with an abdominal bruit and high renin** = renal artery stenosis (renin-driven secondary hypertension).

stem: A 58-year-old woman has blood pressure of 190/110 mm Hg despite three drugs. An abdominal bruit is heard. Labs: potassium 3.0 mEq/L, bicarbonate 32 mEq/L, plasma renin activity high, aldosterone high.
oneliner: 58F + BP 190/110 on three drugs + abdominal bruit + K 3.0, HCO3 32 + high renin and high aldosterone → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **low renin** because the aldosterone is autonomous; renin here is high
whyNot.B: **episodic symptoms and raised metanephrines** without alkalosis; renin and aldosterone are both high here
whyNot.C: **central obesity, striae and raised cortisol**; none described
whyNot.D: **normal renin and potassium** with no bruit; here there is a bruit with secondary hyperaldosteronism

why: **Hypertension with an abdominal bruit, hypokalemic alkalosis and both renin and aldosterone high** = renal artery stenosis (secondary hyperaldosteronism).

stem: A 27-year-old woman has new hypertension of 168/104 mm Hg. A bruit is heard over the left flank, and plasma renin activity is high. Pulses in the arms and legs are equal, she has no episodic headaches or sweating, and there is no family history of hypertension.

ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **low renin and hypokalemia**; renin here is high
whyNot.B: **episodic headaches, sweating and palpitations**; none here
whyNot.C: **family history and onset in middle age** without a bruit; here a young woman has a bruit and high renin
whyNot.E: **weak or delayed femoral pulses** and an arm-leg pressure gradient; pulses here are equal

why: **Young woman with sudden hypertension, flank bruit and high renin** = renal artery stenosis, classically from fibromuscular dysplasia.

stem: A 58-year-old woman has new hypertension of 175/105 mm Hg. CT shows a large retroperitoneal mass pressing on the left renal artery. Renal blood flow and GFR are preserved, and plasma renin activity is high. Urine metanephrines are normal.

ask: Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient's hypertension?

whyNot.B: **episodic catecholamine symptoms** and raised metanephrines; here metanephrines are normal and renin is high
whyNot.C: **low renin** with hypokalemia; renin here is high
whyNot.D: **raised cortisol, central obesity** and striae; none here
whyNot.E: **arm-leg blood pressure gradient and rib notching**; imaging shows renal artery compression instead

why: **Mass narrowing the renal artery, preserved GFR from autoregulation, high renin** = renal artery stenosis causing renin-driven hypertension.

stem: A 61-year-old man has had blood pressure around 190/110 mm Hg for 15 years because he never took his medication. He now has edema, BUN of 70 mg/dL, creatinine of 4.2 mg/dL and about 1 g/day of protein with no red cells. Both kidneys are small and echogenic on ultrasound, his hemoglobin A1c is normal, and there is no papilledema or retinal hemorrhage.

ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **papilledema, retinal hemorrhage and encephalopathy** with fibrinoid necrosis; none here
whyNot.C: **hematuria with RBC casts** and proteinuria; his sediment has no red cells
whyNot.D: **large cystic kidneys** and a family history; his kidneys are small

why: **Long-standing uncontrolled hypertension with chronic renal failure, mild proteinuria and small kidneys** = hypertensive nephrosclerosis (hyaline arteriolosclerosis).

stem: A 70-year-old man with atrial fibrillation who is not on anticoagulants has sudden severe left flank pain, nausea and gross hematuria. LDH is 1,100 U/L. He dies suddenly of a stroke 2 days later. A photograph of the cut surface of his left kidney at autopsy is shown.

whyNot.A: **a round yellow mass** that bulges and invades the renal vein; the lesion here is not a tumor mass
whyNot.B: **sloughed papillae** at the tips of the pyramids with diabetes or analgesics; the damage here is cortical
whyNot.D: **multiple cysts** replacing the parenchyma; none seen
whyNot.E: **pus-filled cavity** with fever and bacteria; the lesion here is solid and pale

stem: A 2-week-old boy has had severe diarrhea for 2 days and is dehydrated. He now has gross hematuria and a palpable, enlarged right flank mass, and platelets are 60,000/mm3. Doppler ultrasound shows an enlarged, echogenic right kidney with absent venous flow; arterial flow is present.
oneliner: 2-week M + dehydrating diarrhea + gross hematuria, enlarged flank mass + low platelets + Doppler: absent renal venous flow, arterial flow present → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **absent arterial flow** with a small, ischemic kidney; here arterial flow is present
whyNot.C: **oliguria with muddy brown casts** and no flank mass or vein clot
whyNot.D: **solid mass in a well child**, not an echogenic kidney with a venous clot after dehydration
whyNot.E: **dilated collecting system** without hematuria or thrombocytopenia; here the kidney is echogenic with no venous flow

why: **Dehydrated neonate with hematuria, an enlarged kidney, low platelets and absent renal venous flow** = renal vein thrombosis.

stem: A 24-year-old woman has had burning on urination, urinary frequency and urgency for 2 days. She is afebrile and has suprapubic tenderness but no flank pain. Urinalysis is positive for nitrite and leukocyte esterase.
oneliner: 24F + dysuria + frequency + urgency 2 d + suprapubic tenderness + no fever or flank pain + nitrite/LE positive → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **No fever and no flank pain or CVA tenderness**; infection is limited to the bladder
whyNot.C: **Nitrite-positive urine with suprapubic tenderness** points to a bacterial bladder infection; chlamydia gives sterile pyuria with a gradual onset
whyNot.D: **Acute 2-day onset with infected urine**; interstitial cystitis is chronic bladder pain with sterile urine
whyNot.E: **No colicky pain or hematuria**; pain is suprapubic, not flank-to-groin

why: **Dysuria, frequency, urgency and suprapubic tenderness without fever or flank pain**, with **nitrite and leukocyte esterase in the urine** = acute cystitis, usually E. coli.

stem: A 58-year-old wheelchair-bound man with a spinal cord injury has had his third urinary infection this year, each treated with a short antibiotic course. He now has burning on urination and urinary frequency but no fever or flank pain, and his prostate is nontender. Urinalysis shows pyuria, and culture grows E. coli resistant to ciprofloxacin.
oneliner: 58M + wheelchair-bound + 3rd UTI this year + dysuria + frequency + afebrile + nontender prostate + pyuria, E. coli cipro-resistant → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **No fever, flank pain or CVA tenderness**; symptoms are confined to the bladder
whyNot.B: **Prostate is nontender** and he has no fever or perineal pain

whyNot.E: **Infected urine with pyuria and a positive culture**; interstitial cystitis has sterile urine

stem: A 26-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation has had fever, nausea and right flank pain for 2 days. Temperature is 39.4 C, blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg, and the uterus is nontender with intact membranes. There is right costovertebral angle tenderness and the urine shows pyuria with white cell casts.
oneliner: 26F + 30 wk pregnant + fever 39.4 + right flank pain + CVA tenderness + pyuria with WBC casts + normal BP + nontender uterus → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Fever, flank pain and CVA tenderness** mean the kidney is involved, not just the bladder
whyNot.C: **Fever with pyuria and WBC casts**, not afebrile colicky pain radiating to the groin.
whyNot.D: **Blood pressure is normal**; preeclampsia requires hypertension.
whyNot.E: **Uterus is nontender with intact membranes**; the tenderness is in the costovertebral angle

why: **Fever, flank pain and CVA tenderness with pyuria and WBC casts in pregnancy** = acute pyelonephritis.

stem: A 22-year-old woman had 3 days of burning on urination and urinary frequency, and now has fever of 38.9 C and right flank pain. There is right costovertebral angle tenderness. Urine microscopy shows pyuria, and Gram stain of the urine shows gram-negative rods. She is not sexually active and has no vaginal discharge.
oneliner: 22F + dysuria + frequency then fever + right flank pain + CVA tenderness + gram-negative rods in urine → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Fever and CVA tenderness** show upper tract involvement
whyNot.B: **Fever and bacteriuria** with preceding dysuria; stones cause afebrile colicky pain
whyNot.C: **Right flank (CVA) tenderness with pyuria and bacteria in the urine**, not right lower quadrant pain
whyNot.D: **No vaginal discharge, not sexually active**, and the urine is full of gram-negative rods

stem: A 71-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia has had fever of 39 C and right flank pain for 2 days. He has right costovertebral angle tenderness. The prostate is mildly enlarged, smooth and nontender. Urinalysis shows pyuria, and culture grows gram-positive cocci in chains.
oneliner: 71M + BPH + fever 39 + right flank pain + CVA tenderness + pyuria + gram-positive cocci in urine + nontender prostate → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Fever and CVA tenderness** show kidney involvement
whyNot.B: **Prostate is nontender** and there is no perineal pain
whyNot.D: **Fever with pyuria and positive culture** rather than afebrile colicky pain
whyNot.E: **Acute fever with pyuria and bacteriuria**, no hematuria or flank mass

why: **Fever, flank pain and CVA tenderness with pyuria** and a positive urine culture = acute pyelonephritis; BPH-related incomplete emptying predisposes to it, and a gram-positive organism such as Enterococcus can be the cause.

stem: A 68-year-old woman has fever, rigors and right flank pain. Temperature is 39.2 C and there is right costovertebral angle tenderness. Urine is positive for nitrite and leukocyte esterase. White cell count is 55,000/microL. A peripheral blood smear is shown.
oneliner: 68F + fever + rigors + flank pain + CVA tenderness + nitrite/LE positive urine + WBC 55,000 + [blood smear] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Acute fever with CVA tenderness and infected urine**; CML is usually indolent with splenomegaly and basophilia
whyNot.C: **Very high WBC from infection**; MDS causes cytopenias with dysplastic cells
whyNot.D: **No blasts on the smear**; the neutrophils are mature with a left shift
whyNot.E: **Neutrophilic left shift, not atypical lymphocytes**, and a urinary source of infection

stem: A 64-year-old man with a history of kidney stones has passed no urine for 24 hours and has mild lower abdominal discomfort. Blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg. stem: A 28-year-old man had a motorcycle crash with a pelvic fracture 3 weeks ago. He now has constant dribbling of urine and lower abdominal fullness. The bladder is palpable, a catheter passes easily and drains 600 mL, and cystometry shows no detrusor contraction when the bladder is filled.
